items.title: Verbose error messages and stack traces disclose sensitive internals
items.claim: Verbose error messages and stack traces disclose sensitive internals.
items.body: Applications that return detailed error responses - stack traces, database or OS error text, debug pages - disclose the technology stack, file paths, and internal state to any attacker able to trigger the error. CWE-200 covers incidental exposure; CWE-209 specifically addresses generation of error messages containing sensitive information.
items.disproof: Refuted if the exposure vector is removed: generic error responses, disabled directory listing, non-URL session exchange, allowlisted Host for password resets, excluded backup/.git files, no hardcoded secrets, sanitized version banners and patched frameworks.

sources.quote: Explicitly mentioning database table or column names in error messages
the code manages resources that intentionally contain sensitive information, but the resources are unintentionally made accessible to unauthorized actors

Verbose error messages can also provide information about different technologies being used by the website. For example, they might explicitly name a template engine, database type, or server that the website is using, along with its version number.

items.title: Directory listings and crawler files expose hidden resources and structure
items.claim: Directory listings and crawler files expose hidden resources and structure.
items.body: Web servers configured to list directory contents, or that reveal crawler files such as robots.txt and sitemap.xml, disclose resource structure and the existence/location of sensitive files.
items.disproof: Refuted if the exposure vector is removed: generic error responses, disabled directory listing, non-URL session exchange, allowlisted Host for password resets, excluded backup/.git files, no hardcoded secrets, sanitized version banners and patched frameworks.

sources.quote: Revealing the names of hidden directories, their structure, and their contents via a robots.txt file or directory listing
Disable web server directory listing and ensure file metadata (e.g., .git) and backup files are not present within web roots.

Directory listings themselves are not necessarily a security vulnerability. However, if the website also fails to implement proper access control, leaking the existence and location of sensitive resources in this way is clearly an issue.

items.title: Session IDs and credentials exposed via URLs, logs, and Referer headers
items.claim: Session IDs and credentials exposed via URLs, logs, and Referer headers.
items.body: When the session ID is sent in a URL parameter, it is written to browser history, bookmarks, referring sites, proxy and web server logs, and may be leaked through the Referer header.
items.disproof: Refuted if the exposure vector is removed: generic error responses, disabled directory listing, non-URL session exchange, allowlisted Host for password resets, excluded backup/.git files, no hardcoded secrets, sanitized version banners and patched frameworks.

sources.quote: The usage of specific session ID exchange mechanisms, such as those where the ID is included in the URL, might disclose the session ID.

items.title: Password reset poisoning via Host header rewrites reset links
items.claim: Password reset poisoning via Host header rewrites reset links.
items.body: If the password reset email URL is built from attacker-influenced Host/header values, the victim receives a reset link pointing to the attacker domain, carrying a valid token.
items.disproof: Refuted if the exposure vector is removed: generic error responses, disabled directory listing, non-URL session exchange, allowlisted Host for password resets, excluded backup/.git files, no hardcoded secrets, sanitized version banners and patched frameworks.

sources.quote: Password reset poisoning is a technique whereby an attacker manipulates a vulnerable website into generating a password reset link pointing to a domain under their control.

items.title: Source code disclosure via backup files, temp files, and .git metadata
items.claim: Source code disclosure via backup files, temp files, and .git metadata.
items.body: Temporary backup files (e.g., .bak, ~ suffix), source files placed under web roots, and exposed .git directories let attackers download application source, including hard-coded credentials and internal paths.
items.disproof: Refuted if the exposure vector is removed: generic error responses, disabled directory listing, non-URL session exchange, allowlisted Host for password resets, excluded backup/.git files, no hardcoded secrets, sanitized version banners and patched frameworks.

sources.quote: Providing access to source code files via temporary backups
Obtaining source code access makes it much easier for an attacker to understand the application behavior and construct high-severity attacks.

items.title: Hard-coded secrets, API keys, and credentials in source code
items.claim: Hard-coded secrets, API keys, and credentials in source code.
items.body: Secrets committed to source code - database credentials, API keys, tokens, private keys - are exposed to anyone who can access the code.
items.disproof: Refuted if the exposure vector is removed: generic error responses, disabled directory listing, non-URL session exchange, allowlisted Host for password resets, excluded backup/.git files, no hardcoded secrets, sanitized version banners and patched frameworks.

sources.quote: Leaked secrets are sensitive credentials, keys, tokens, and other types of authentication means that are unintentionally exposed.
It is important to avoid putting sensitive information such as credentials, API keys, IP addresses, and personal names directly into the code.

items.title: Version disclosure chains to CVE exploitation
items.claim: Version disclosure chains to CVE exploitation.
items.body: Stack traces, Server headers, and error pages disclose the exact framework version; an attacker maps that version to known CVEs.
items.disproof: Refuted if the exposure vector is removed: generic error responses, disabled directory listing, non-URL session exchange, allowlisted Host for password resets, excluded backup/.git files, no hardcoded secrets, sanitized version banners and patched frameworks.

sources.quote: the knowledge that a website is using a particular framework version is of limited use if that version is fully patched.
The Jakarta Multipart parser in Apache Struts 2 2.3.x before 2.3.32 and 2.5.x before 2.5.10.1 has incorrect exception handling and error-message generation
The unexpected data type causes an exception, and a full stack trace is displayed in the response. This reveals that the lab is using Apache Struts 2 2.3.31.
